ITEM 2  Beachfront Definition for Residential Development Standards – Local
  Coastal Program Amendment No. Xx-xxx and Zoning Text Amendment
  No. xx-xxx.

  Recommended Action: Review the proposed definition of “beachfront” for
  inclusion in the Local Coastal Program (LCP) Local Implementation Plan
  (LIP) and Title 17 (Zoning) of the Malibu Municipal Code (MMC) and
  provide feedback for consideration by the Planning Commission.

  Assistant Community Development Director Eaton presented the report.
  Staff is requesting authorization to amend the Local Coastal Program and
  zoning code to clearly define “beachfront.” The purpose is to eliminate
  ambiguity and ensure properties receive the appropriate development
  standards consistently.

  Principal Planner Smith explained that beachfront properties have more
  flexible development standards, including reduced setbacks, greater height,
  and no maximums on impermeable coverage, two third calculations or
  TDSF (Total Development Square Footage). The proposed definition is
  intended to provide consistency while protecting the natural environment,
  rural character, and open-space areas.

  Staff proposed three criteria for determining whether a property is
  beachfront: it must directly border the coast, it cannot have an RR (Rural
  Residential) designation, and its primary use must be in a low-lying
  shoreline area rather than separated from the beach by a bluff, cliff, hill, or
  other elevated coastal landform.

  Staff reviewed photos of properties to differentiate what is considered beach
  front and what is not. They emphasized that simply having a parcel touch
  the beach does not automatically make it beachfront; the property's zoning
  and physical/topographic characteristics also matter.

  Councilmember Uhring questioned whether the definition would be clear
  and easy to apply when property owners challenge the determination. Staff
  explained that the goal is to replace the city's informal historical practice
  with a written standard that can be consistently applied and defended.

  Broad Beach and potential sand-dune changes were also discussed. Staff
  noted that the definition could be adjusted to clarify how sand dunes should
  be treated.

  Finally, staff clarified that an accessory structure located on the beach does
  not make the entire property beachfront if the primary residence or primary
  use is located away from the beach.

  Staff clarified that beach stairs, seawalls, and other accessory structures do
  not determine beachfront status. The primary residence or primary use is
  what matters. Examples showed homes on top of bluffs or elevated areas
  that have accessory structures leading to the beach but would still not
  qualify as beachfront.

  Principal Planner Smith also explained that this has been a long-standing
  issue and that the proposed definition largely formalizes the way the city
  has already been making these determinations. A GIS map could eventually
  show property owners clearly whether their property qualifies. Staff
  recommended taking the proposal to the Planning Commission and then
  back to the City Council.

  Councilmember Uhring emphasized when bringing to the Planning
  Commission to be clear that the proposal is not intended to change existing
  policy, but rather to put the city's long-standing practice into clear written
  rules. Councilmember Uhring supported using the examples and GIS
  mapping to make the rules easier for property owners and staff to
  understand.

MOTION  Councilmember Riggins moved and Mayor Pro Tem Uhring seconded a
  motion to approve staff recommendation of the proposed definition of
  “beachfront” for inclusion in the Local Coastal Program (LCP) Local
  Implementation Plan (LIP) and Title 17 (Zoning) of the Malibu Municipal
  Code (MMC) and direct it to the Planning Commission for consideration.
  The motion carried unanimously.

  Discussion after the motion: Councilmember Uhring suggested keeping the
  presentation's photographs and examples available for future property
  disputes and potentially putting them on the city's website. He also wanted
  to note that no one appeared to attend the meeting specifically to oppose the
  proposal.

Subject:  Mitigation Framework for ESHA and Protected Native Trees

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Review the proposed framework to improve the City’s
review process and mitigation protocol in the Local Coastal Program (LCP) to address
unavoidable impacts on Environmentally Sensitive Habitat Area (ESHA) and protected
native trees resulting from development, and provide guidance to staff on next steps.

DISCUSSION: The proposed framework includes the following three components:

  1. Establish a policy to clarify how the City’s mitigation requirements apply to
  unavoidable impacts to ESHA and native trees (Attachment 1).

  2. Establish a policy to require the City Biologist conduct a site inspection, at the
  applicant’s expense, when impacts to ESHA and native trees may occur
  (Attachment 2).

  3. Initiate an LCP Amendment (LCPA) to change the recipient of in-lieu fees from
  the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy (SMMC) to the City and to ensure
  that the use of funds remains in the City to the maximum extent available.

As outlined below, the proposed framework is intended to improve the City’s mitigation
protocol when ESHA and native tree mitigation is required for new development.

  Item No. 3.B.
  Page 1 of 9

  Page 6 of 19
 Proposed Components of the Framework

Component 1:  Establish a policy to clarify how the City’s mitigation requirements
  apply to unavoidable impacts to ESHA and native trees.

ESHA Component: The LCP requires that new development shall be sited and
designed to avoid impacts to ESHA.1 It further requires that where there is no feasible
alternative that can eliminate all impacts, the alternative that would result in the fewest
or least significant impacts shall be selected. When development results in
unavoidable impacts to ESHA, the LCP mandates that those impacts be fully
mitigated, with priority given to onsite mitigation. Impacts could occur in various forms
of development such as the creation of a driveway, necessary grading to create a
building pad, remediation of a geologic hazard, construction of a structure, voluntary
vegetation management, or required fuel modification. LCP Local Implementation Plan
(LIP) Section 4.8.1 provides three methods to mitigate ESHA impacts: 1) habitat
restoration; 2) habitat conservation; or 3) an in-lieu fee for habitat conservation.

Native Tree Component: The LCP requires that new development shall be sited and
designed to avoid impacts to native trees2 to the maximum extent feasible. It further
requires that where there is no feasible alternative that can prevent tree removal or
encroachment, then the alternative that would result in the fewest or least significant
impacts shall be selected. When development results in unavoidable impacts to native
trees, the LCP mandates that those impacts be fully mitigated, with priority given to
onsite mitigation. LIP Section 5.5 provides three methods to mitigate for native tree
impacts: 1) onsite tree replacement at a 10 to 1 ratio; 2) offsite mitigation at a 10 to 1
ratio on a site that is restricted from development or is public parkland; and 3) an in-
lieu fee to restore or create native tree woodland or savannah habitat.

LIP Chapters 4 (ESHA) and 5 (Native Tree Protection) emphasize the importance of
fully mitigating impacts onsite. LIP Section 4.8(A) stipulates that offsite mitigation is
only permitted when onsite mitigation proves infeasible. Additionally, LCP Land Use
Policy (LUP) Policy 3.51 mandates that measures to restore disturbed or degraded
habitat on the affected property must be included as mitigation when new development
removes or adversely impacts native vegetation.

Despite the LCP’s emphasis for onsite mitigation, it is staff’s experience that the
methods described in LIP Sections 4.8.1 (ESHA) and 5.5 (native trees) are often
viewed by the public as a menu of mitigation options rather than a mitigation hierarchy.
In practice, this view has resulted in the many applications proposing in-lieu fees
without first documenting whether restoration or conservation on the subject parcel, or

1
  LIP §2.1 defines ESHA as “any area in which plant or animal life or their habitats are either rare or especially valuable
because of their special nature or role in an ecosystem and which could be easily disturbed or degraded by human
activities and developments.” Additional criteria to be used when determining ESHA is provided in LIP §4.3(B).
2
  LIP §5.1 defines native trees as native oak, walnut, sycamore, alder, and toyon, where there is at least one trunk
measuring six inches or more in diameter, or a combination of any two trunks measuring a total of eight inches or more in
diameter, measured at four and one-half feet above natural grade.
  Page 2 of 9  Item No. 3.B.
  Page 7 of 19
 offsite location, is achievable.3 Because the LIP does not explicitly require an applicant
to demonstrate infeasibility for each mitigation method before considering the next, it
can be challenging to compel an applicant to use a more protective mitigation method
without a definitive City policy on the matter. As a result, impacts to ESHA and native
trees that occur within the City are not always offset within the City. The in lieu fees go
to outside agencies that use the funds to support habitat restoration and
implementation projects in the Santa Monica Mountains but it may not directly result
in improving habitats in the City. Further, the City does not have a clear mechanism in
the LIP to require that mitigation be provided in proximity to the ESHA or native trees
that were impacted by development.

The policy mandates that ESHA and native tree mitigation is provided in a hierarchy,
with methods based on an order of priority. The policy allows an applicant to propose
any mitigation method only upon demonstrating, with substantial evidence and subject
to the City Biologist’s and the Community Development Director’s review and
acceptance, that each higher mitigation method is infeasible. If an applicant is unable
to demonstrate infeasibility, then the higher method would be required to mitigate for
impacts. This hierarchy will help staff provide concrete guidance to applicants and
ensure the majority of the mitigation/restoration, if not all, happens within the City of
Malibu.

The mitigation hierarchy is:

  Method 1.  Complete avoidance of ESHA/protected native trees wherever
  feasible.

  Method 2.  Onsite mitigation on the subject parcel, through habitat restoration
  or habitat conservation, at the required ratios indicated in the LIP
  Chapters 4 and 5 respectively. This method is strongly preferred
  and would be the default expectation for all projects.

  Method 3.  Offsite mitigation at a location within the City, where onsite
  mitigation is demonstrated to be infeasible. This method gives
  strong preference that the offsite location be as close to the area
  impacted as feasible.

  Method 4.  Offsite mitigation at a location within the Santa Monica Mountains
  Coastal Zone in close proximity to the City, where no feasible
  mitigation opportunity exists within the City.

3
  Two common reasons why an applicant desires to pay an in-lieu fee are: 1) less burdensome than restoration or
conserving land; and 2) restoration may fail following installation. Regarding restoration performance, the LIP contains
implementation safeguards that address this concern. LIP §4.8.1(A)(2) requires two performance bonds prior to building
permit issuance, one for labor and materials and one for five years of maintenance and monitoring and authorizes the City
to collect the security and complete the work on the property if the applicant fails to perform.
  Page 3 of 9  Item No. 3.B.
  Page 8 of 19
   Method 5.  Payment of an in-lieu fee, only where mitigation is demonstrated to
  be infeasible at each of the higher tiers. This method would be
  considered a last resort and would not be accepted by the City as
  a matter of applicant preference, cost, or convenience.

  Method 6.  A combination of the hierarchy in this order.

Some lots that cannot accommodate a full onsite replacement may substitute some
onsite mitigation for offsite mitigation first, then in lieu fees if there are no other options
(Method 6). After all, within City boundaries there are a plethora of sensitive habitats
that can use restoration and/or mitigative improvements. For example, if two native
protected trees were impacted from a development project, the LIP requires that the
trees be replaced at a 10:1 ratio, so 20 trees of the same species would need to be
planted and monitored for their survival over the course of a 10-year period. If the lot
was smaller and only could accommodate the planting of 12 trees onsite, and the
applicant proves with substantial evidence that the remaining onsite mitigation is not
feasible, they would be required to locate an alternative site within the City to plant the
remaining 8 trees before turning to in lieu fees.

The policy clarifies the City’s expectations to applicants and the public, and would also
be used by staff and the City’s decision makers when reviewing coastal development
permit (CDP) applications. In particular, the policy would guide the City’s determination
when making the third finding required for all CDPs – that the project is the least
environmentally damaging alternative (LIP Section 13.9(C)). If the City’s decision
makers find that a higher ESHA mitigation method is feasible and available to an
applicant, but it was not adequately considered, the project’s approval may be
conditioned to require the higher method or denied since the finding in LIP Section
13.9(C) cannot be made. Specific to native trees, LIP Section 5.7(C) requires a finding
that all feasible mitigation measures that would substantially lessen significant impacts
have been incorporated. Similarly, if the City’s decision makers find that a higher native
tree mitigation method is feasible and available to an applicant, but it was not
adequately considered, the project’s approval may be conditioned to require the higher
method or denied since the finding in LIP Section 5.7(C) cannot be made.

Component 1 is already being practiced by staff but could be formalized as an official
City policy by the end of 2026 with the Planning Commission’s adoption of a formal
policy. This is because the LIP and LUP have existing language to support the
hierarchy without need for an LCPA.4 A draft policy is included as Attachment 1 for
ZORACES’ review and consideration.

4
  An LCPA is required only where the City proposes to change the text of the LCP or to apply a standard the LCP does
not support. Neither of the policies described in Components 1 and 2 do so. The first policy states the priority for onsite
mitigation is already established by LIP §§4.8(A) and 5.5 and LUP Policies 3.14 and 3.51, and the inspection policy
applies the City Biologist review already required by LIP §§4.3(D) and 5.8(B). Both rest on authority the LCP already
assigns to the City, including the Planning Commission's authority to find conformance with the LCP (LIP §§13.7(B) and
13.9(A) and (D)), to impose conditions necessary to ensure LCP conformance (LIP §13.8), and to require supporting
information and fees (LIP §§13.6.1(A) and 13.6.3; LUP Policy 3.39)
  Page 4 of 9  Item No. 3.B.
  Page 9 of 19
 Component 2:  Establish a policy to require the City Biologist conduct a site
  inspection, at the applicant’s expense, when impacts to ESHA and
  native trees may occur.

LIP Section 4.3(A) requires the City to determine the physical extent of habitat that
meets the LIP’s definition of ESHA on a project site. This determination is based on
the applicant’s site-specific biological study and other relevant sources. Additionally,
LIP Section 4.3(D) requires that the City must make findings regarding the physical
extent of ESHA present. These findings are based on the applicant’s study and other
relevant sources, and reviews by the City Biologist and the Environmental Review
Board (ERB).

Historically, the City requires an onsite investigation by the City Biologist for projects
with the potential to affect ESHA and native trees, but this requirement is not expressly
stated in LIP Chapters 4 or 5. The policy memorializes the City's longstanding practice
and clarifies to applicants that the City Biologist is expected to conduct a site visit at
the applicant’s expense. The City Biologist’s review of a project site is important
because relying upon a review of maps and records alone is not a sufficient basis for
the findings required by LIP Sections 4.3(D) and 5.7. The City Biologist would conduct
the inspection and prepare a written ESHA determination identifying habitat types
observed, the mapped extent of ESHA, protected native trees and their protected
zones, applicable buffers under LIP Section 4.6.1, and the preliminary applicability of
LIP Sections 4.6, 4.7, 4.8 and Chapter 5. The determination would be transmitted to
the project planner and the applicant and incorporated into the staff report and any
recommended conditions of approval.

Component 2 is already being practiced by staff but could be formalized as official
policy by the end of 2026 with the Planning Commission’s adoption of a formal policy.
This is because the LIP and LUP have existing language to support City Biologist site
inspections without need for an LCPA. A draft policy is included as Attachment 2 for
ZORACES’ review and consideration.

Component 3:  Initiate an LCPA to change the recipient of in-lieu fees from the
  SMMC to the City and to ensure that the use of funds remains in
  the City to the maximum extent available.

When in-lieu fees are paid by an applicant, LIP Sections 4.8.1(C)(2) and 5.5.2, and
LUP Policy 3.66, state that the fees may used to restore or conserve habitat anywhere
within the Santa Monica Mountains Coastal Zone. The LIP does not prioritize the use
of funds within the City but does require that fees shall be used within the Santa Monica
Mountains for the acquisition or permanent preservation of properties containing areas
designated ESHA, and to properties contiguous with existing parklands containing
natural habitat. Additionally, the LCP designates the SMMC as the recipient of the
funds, not the City.

  Page 5 of 9  Item No. 3.B.
  Page 10 of 19
 LIP Sections 4.8.1(C)(2) and 5.5.2 and LUP Policy 3.66 stipulate that in-lieu fees be
paid into the Habitat Impact Mitigation Fund (ESHA) and Native Tree Impact Mitigation
Fund (native trees), both of which are administered by the SMMC. Therefore, if the
City desires to be the recipient of these fees, an LCPA would be required since the
SMMC is named as the administering agency for in-lieu fees. Fees collected by the
City would be held in a designated account and used for conservation of land,
consistent with the LCP. The goal of the LCPA would ensure that mitigation for ESHA
and native tree impacts remains within the City to the maximum extent available.

Staff suggests the LCPA include the following components:

  1. Designate the City as recipient of in-lieu fees for ESHA and native tree
  mitigation;

  2. Prioritize the expenditure of funds must be within the City of Malibu before
  use elsewhere within the Santa Monica Mountains;

  3. Authorize the City Manager to have the ability to transfer funds to a public
  agency or nonprofit organization by written agreement when the City cannot
  find a proper location for fund expenditure itself(e.g., SMMC);

  4. Require annual public reporting; and

  5. Prohibit transfer of funds into the City’s General Fund.

The LCP has precedent for naming the City as recipient for in-lieu fees and
conservation easements. LIP Section 12.10 designates the City as recipient of in-lieu
fees paid for new luxury overnight accommodations. Those fees are held by the City
in a fund to subsidize the construction of lower cost overnight facilities in the Malibu-
Santa Monica Mountains Coastal Zone area of Los Angeles County or Ventura
County. Pursuant to LIP Section 12.10(C), the City may transfer funds to a public
agency, nonprofit organization, or private entity by memorandum of understanding.
LIP Section 4.8.1(B)(1)(a) requires that permanent, irrevocable open space
easements associated with habitat conservation be dedicated to and enforceable by
the City.

This component requires initiation by the City Council to start the LCPA process. Once
prepared, the LCPA would be reviewed by the Planning Commission and
recommendations provided to the City Council. If adopted by the City Council, the
LCPA would be submitted to the California Coastal Commission (CCC) for certification
in the LCP. The LCPA would not be effective unless and until the LCPA certification
process was completed.

  Page 6 of 9  Item No. 3.B.
  Page 11 of 19
 General Plan & LCP Consistency

The following General Plan Conservation (CON) Element and LUP policies support
the proposed mitigation framework.

General Plan

  1. CON Policy 1.1.4: The City shall protect ESHAs as a priority over development
  and against any significant disruption of habitat values.

  2. CON Policy 1.1.2: The City shall protect riparian areas and undisturbed areas
  within significant watersheds and wildlife habitat linkages through the use of
  open space or conservation easements or equivalent measures.

  3. CON Policy 1.1.6: The City shall restore Disturbed Sensitive Resource Areas to
  the extent feasible and ecologically desirable.

  4. CON Policy 1.2.1: The City shall preserve wildlife habitats and habitat linkages.

  5. CON Policy 1.2.3: The City shall mitigate net loss of very threatened plant
  communities.

LUP

  1. Policy 3.14: New development shall be sited and designed to avoid impacts to
  ESHA. If there is no feasible alternative that can eliminate all impacts, then the
  alternative that would result in the fewest or least significant impacts shall be
  selected. Impacts to ESHA that cannot be avoided through the implementation
  of siting and design alternatives shall be fully mitigated, with priority given to on-
  site mitigation. Off-site mitigation measures shall only be approved when it is
  not feasible to fully mitigate impacts on-site or where off-site mitigation is more
  protective in the context of a Natural Community Conservation Plan that is
  certified by the Commission as an amendment to the LCP. Mitigation shall not
  substitute for implementation of the project alternative that would avoid impacts
  to ESHA.

  2. Policy 3.51: Disturbed areas’ ESHAs shall not be further degraded, and if
  feasible, restored. If new development removes or adversely impacts native
  vegetation, measures to restore any disturbed or degraded habitat on the
  property shall be included as mitigation.

  3. Policy 3.30: Protection of ESHA and public access shall take priority over other
  development standards and where there is any conflict between general
  development standards and ESHA and/or public access protection, the
  standards that are most protective of ESHA and public access shall have
  precedence.
  Page 7 of 9  Item No. 3.B.
  Page 12 of 19
   4. Policy 3.39 (excerpt): The ERB, in consultation with the City Biologist, shall
  review development within or adjacent to designated ESHA or other areas
  containing ESHA identified through a biological study as required pursuant to
  Policy 3.37. The City may impose a fee on applicants to recover the cost of
  review of a proposed project by the ERB when required by this policy.

  5. Policy 3.65: Where the removal of native trees cannot be avoided through the
  implementation of project alternatives or where development encroachments
  into the protected zone of native trees result in the loss or worsened health of
  the trees, mitigation measures shall include, at a minimum, the planting of
  replacement trees on-site, if suitable area exists on the project site, at a ratio of
  10 replacement trees for every 1 tree removed. Where on-site mitigation is not
  feasible, off-site mitigation shall be provided through planting replacement trees
  or by providing an in-lieu fee, based on the type, size and age of the tree(s)
  removed.

ZORACES Request

ZORACES is requested to provide staff guidance on the following:

  1. Feedback on the proposed mitigation framework: 1) policy clarifying the
  mitigation hierarchy; 2) policy requiring City Biologist inspections; and 3) LCPA
  to designate the City as recipient of in-lieu fees.

  2. If it is acceptable for the Planning Commission to be the entity that considers
  the two policies for adoption, or if the two policies should be elevated to the City
  Council for consideration and adoption.

  3. Recommend the City Council initiates the LCPA to change the recipient of in-
  lieu fees from the SMMC to the City and to ensure that the use of funds remains
  in the City to the maximum extent available.

Next Steps

Based on the input received by the Subcommittee, the Planning Division would:

  1. Finalize draft policies for Components 1 and 2 to be presented to the Planning
  Commission (or City Council) for adoption.

  2. Request the City Council initiate an LCPA to the LIP and LUP to change the
  recipient of in-lieu fees from the SMMC to the City and to ensure that the use of
  funds remains in the City to the maximum extent available. If initiated, the
  Planning Division would prepare an LCPA and present it to the Planning
  Commission for review and recommendation to the City Council. If adopted by
  the City Council, the LCPA would be submitted to the CCC for certification in the

   LCP. The LCPA would not be effective unless and until the LCPA certification
  process was completed.

  MMC and LCP Sections: LIP Chapters 4 (Environmentally Sensitive Habitat Overlay) and 5 Native Tree
  Protection Ordinance

  Title: Mitigation Hierarchy for ESHA & Native Trees

  The Local Coastal Program (LCP) requires that new development shall be sited and
  designed to avoid impacts to Environmentally Sensitive Habitat Area (ESHA). It
  further requires that where there is no feasible alternative that can eliminate all
  impacts, the alternative that would result in the fewest or least significant impacts
  shall be selected. When development results in unavoidable impacts to ESHA, the
  LCP mandates that those impacts be fully mitigated, with priority given to onsite
  mitigation. LCP Local Implementation Plan (LIP) §4.8.1 provides three methods to
  mitigate ESHA impacts: 1) habitat restoration; 2) habitat conservation; or 3) an in-
  lieu fee for habitat conservation.

  The LCP requires that new development shall be sited and designed to avoid
  impacts to native trees to the maximum extent feasible. It further requires that where
  there is no feasible alternative that can prevent tree removal or encroachment, then
  the alternative that would result in the fewest or least significant impacts shall be
  selected. When development results in unavoidable impacts to native trees, the
  LCP mandates that those impacts be fully mitigated, with priority given to onsite
  mitigation. LIP §5.5 provides three methods to mitigate for native tree impacts: 1)
  onsite tree replacement at a 10 to 1 ratio; 2) offsite mitigation at a 10 to 1 ratio on a
  site that is restricted from development or is public parkland; and 3) an in-lieu fee to
  restore or create native tree woodland or savannah habitat.

 LIP Chapters 4 (ESHA) and 5 (Native Tree Protection) emphasize the importance
of fully mitigating impacts onsite. LIP §4.8(A) stipulates that offsite mitigation is only
permitted when onsite mitigation proves infeasible. Additionally, LCP Land Use
Policy (LUP) Policy 3.51 mandates that measures to restore disturbed or degraded
habitat on the affected property must be included as mitigation when new
development removes or adversely impacts native vegetation.

Application

ESHA and native tree mitigation shall be provided in a hierarchy, with methods
based on an order of priority. A project applicant may propose any mitigation method
but only upon demonstrating, with substantial evidence and subject to the City
Biologist’s review and acceptance, that each higher method is infeasible. If an
applicant is unable to demonstrate infeasibility, then the higher method would be
required to mitigate for impacts.

Mitigation Hierarchy:

Method 1. Complete avoidance of ESHA/protected native trees wherever feasible.

Method 2. Onsite mitigation on the subject parcel, through habitat restoration or
  habitat conservation, at the required ratios indicated in the LIP Chapters
  4 and 5 respectively. This method is strongly preferred and would be
  the default expectation for all projects.

Method 3. Offsite mitigation at a location within the City, where onsite mitigation is
  demonstrated to be infeasible. This method gives strong preference that
  the offsite location be as close to the area impacted as feasible.

Method 4. Offsite mitigation at a location within the Santa Monica Mountains
  Coastal Zone in close proximity to the City, where no feasible mitigation
  opportunity exists within the City.

Method 5. Payment of an in-lieu fee, only where mitigation is demonstrated to be
  infeasible at each of the higher tiers. This method would be considered
  a last resort and would not be accepted by the City as a matter of
  applicant preference, cost, or convenience.

Method 6. A combination of the hierarchy in this order.

 Some lots that cannot accommodate a full onsite replacement may substitute some onsite
mitigation for offsite mitigation first, then in-lieu fees if there are no other options (Method
6). After all, within City boundaries there are a plethora of sensitive habitats that can use
restoration and/or mitigative improvements. For example, if two native protected trees
were impacted from a development project the LIP requires that the trees be replaced at
a 10:1 ratio, so 20 trees of the same species would need to be planted and monitored for
their survival over the course of a 10-year period. If the lot was smaller and only could
accommodate the planting of 12 trees onsite, and the applicant proves with substantial
evidence that the remaining onsite mitigation is not feasible, they would be required to
locate an alternative site within the City to plant the remaining 8 trees before turning to in-
lieu fees.

City Determinations on Coastal Development Permits (CDP)

This policy also provides guidance to staff and the City’s decision makers when reviewing
CDP applications. In particular, the policy guides the City’s determination when making
the third finding required for all CDPs – that the project is the least environmentally
damaging alternative (LIP §13.9(C)).

For impacts to ESHA, if the City’s decision makers find that a higher mitigation method is
feasible for and available to an applicant, but it was not adequately considered, the
project’s approval may be conditioned to require the higher method or denied since the
finding in LIP §13.9(C) cannot be made.

For impacts to native trees, LIP §5.7(C) requires a finding that all feasible mitigation
measures that would substantially lessen significant impacts have been incorporated. If
the City’s decision makers find that a higher mitigation method is feasible and available to
an applicant, but it was not adequately considered, the project’s approval may be
conditioned to require the higher method or denied since the finding in LIP §5.7(C) cannot
be made.

  Title: Inspections by the City Biologist

  Local Coastal Program (LCP) Local Implementation Plan (LIP) §4.3 requires the City to
  determine the physical extent of habitat that meets the LIP’s definition of Environmentally
  Sensitive Habitat Area (ESHA) on a project site. This determination is based on the
  applicant’s site-specific biological study and other relevant sources. Additionally, LIP
  Chapter 5 requires the protection of native trees subject to a tree protection plan and tree
  assessment. The City Biologist reviews site-specific studies, biological records, tree
  protection plans, and assessments, and applies applicable LCP provisions. If ESHA or
  native trees are present, the City Biologist determines its extent and the application of LIP
  requirements, including development standards (LIP §§4.6 and 5.4), economically viable
  use provisions (LIP §4.7), and mitigation requirements (LIP §§4.8 and 5.5).

  Application

  To verify the presence of ESHA or native trees and to verify the evidence presented in a
  biological study, an in-person inspection is mandatory for all proposed development where
  ESHA or native trees are documented, mapped, or has the potential to qualify as ESHA
  or a native tree(s). Project applicants must submit payment for the City Biologist inspection
  fee according to the City’s current fee schedule, as adopted by the City Council.

 Procedure

1. If the project contains mapped ESHA or the project materials indicate the potential
  presence of ESHA or Native Protected Trees, the City Biologist will coordinate a site
  inspection with the project applicant and include an invoice with the inspection fee.
2. Applicant shall submit payment and notify the City Biologist.
3. City Biologist will conduct the site inspection and document the City’s records.
4. City Biologist will notify the project planner and applicant of the determination in writing
  confirming or rebutting the evidence presented in the biological study/native tree
  survey.
5. If additional site inspections are warranted, the City Biologist may request additional
  site inspections pursuant to this policy.
